Temples with central wooden pillars on stone bases, like the one at Tell Qasile, illustrate how pulling two pillars could bring down a roof. 27543:
Ruth was a Moabite widow who refused to abandon her bereaved Israelite mother-in-law Naomi. Her vow, 'whither thou goest, I will go... thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God', is one of the most famous declarations of loyalty in literature. In Bethlehem she gleaned barley in the field of Boaz, a wealthy relative of Naomi's husband. Through a bold night-time appeal at the threshing floor, she became his wife under Israel's customs of kinsman-redemption.

The short book that bears her name is set 'in the days when the judges ruled', but it is a sharp contrast to the violence of Judges. Ordinary people show hesed (steadfast covenant love) to one another, and God works quietly through harvest, chance and law rather than through miracles. The Hebrew text even calls her a woman of noble character (eshet chayil), the same phrase as Proverbs 31.

Ruth's Moabite origin is striking because Deuteronomy 23:3 excludes Moabites from the assembly. Her story has been read as showing how faith and loyalty bring a foreigner fully into Israel. She became great-grandmother of King David, and Matthew lists her among the four women in Jesus' genealogy.
27544: She was a Moabitess, widow of Mahlon, and vowed to go with Naomi and take her God. She gleaned in Boaz's field, appealed to him at the threshing floor as redeemer, and married him. She bore Obed, father of Jesse, father of David. The text calls her a virtuous woman and says she was better to Naomi than seven sons.
27545: Ruth is the model convert (giyoret). Her vow is the basis for later conversion practice, and the book is read at Shavuot, the feast of the giving of Torah and of the harvest. The rabbis resolved the tension with Deuteronomy 23 by reading the exclusion as applying to Moabite men only (Mishnah, *Yevamot* 8:3).
27546: Ruth is a figure of the Gentile Church joined to Christ, the true kinsman-redeemer, and an ancestor honoured on the Sunday of the Holy Forefathers. Her loyalty is held up as a model of faithful love.
27547: The book shows God's hidden providence ('her hap was to light on' Boaz's field) and grace to outsiders. Boaz as redeemer (go'el) pictures Christ, who redeems at personal cost.
27548: Many scholars date the book to the post-exilic period and read it as a gentle counter-voice to Ezra–Nehemiah's ban on foreign wives. Others date it to the monarchy (perhaps for legitimising David's line) on linguistic and thematic grounds. The genealogy (Ruth 4:18-22) may be a later appendix.

27557: Marriage and the birth of Obed

Ruth's case combines these customs in a way scholars still discuss. Moab and Israel were related peoples (Gen 19:37) and frequent enemies. Business at the city gate before elders was the normal legal setting.
27559: Ruth's vow is often read at weddings, though originally spoken between two women. The book is read on Shavuot. She is one of the four women named in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, with Tamar, Rahab and Bathsheba, all of whom have unusual or foreign connections. She stands as Scripture's model of loyalty and of the inclusion of the nations.

27667:
Hannah is the woman whose anguished prayer opens the books of Samuel. Childless and mocked by her husband's other wife, she pours out her grief at the Shiloh sanctuary and vows to give a son back to the LORD. God answers, and she hands the young Samuel over to Eli to serve at the sanctuary for life.

Her song (1 Sam 2:1-10) is one of the theological keys to the books that follow. It celebrates a God who brings low and raises up, who feeds the hungry and empties the full, and it ends with the first mention in Samuel of the LORD's king, his anointed one. The reversals she sings about play out in the stories of Eli and Samuel, Saul and David.

She is also an example of honest prayer: she does not hide her bitterness, she persists year after year, and she keeps a costly vow once her prayer is answered.
27668: Wife of Elkanah of Ramathaim-zophim; barren while Peninnah had children (1 Sam 1:2). She prayed silently at Shiloh, vowed her son to the LORD, bore Samuel, gave him to Eli once he was weaned, and sang a prayer (1 Sam 2:1-10). Afterwards she bore three sons and two daughters (1 Sam 2:21).
27669: The Talmud (Berakhot 31a-b) derives rules for the Amidah prayer from Hannah: praying with directed heart, moving the lips while keeping the voice inaudible. Her story is read as the haftarah on the first day of Rosh Hashanah, linked with the idea that God remembers the barren on that day.
27670: Hannah is read as a type of Mary; the Magnificat (Luke 1:46-55) closely echoes her song. Orthodox liturgy uses the Song of Hannah among the biblical odes sung at Matins.
27671: Hannah is often held up as a model of persistent, honest prayer and of entrusting children to God, and her song as a summary of God's preference for the humble.
27673: Many scholars think the song was an older royal psalm placed in Hannah's mouth by the editor, noting its reference to a king (1 Sam 2:10); others argue it fits its setting as anticipatory prophecy. Both views agree it frames the book's theme of reversal.
27674: Brings real grief to God instead of hiding it
27676: Theological depth: her song anticipates the monarchy
27677: The text records no notable failure; she is portrayed as wholly sympathetic

27682: Her song is echoed in Mary's Magnificat and in Christian and Jewish liturgy. She stands in the line of barren mothers through whom God gives a key child: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Samson's mother, Elizabeth.
27683: Rabbinic tradition counts Hannah among the seven women prophets of Israel.
27684: Quiet but intense; speaks plainly about her sorrow, then breaks into confident, poetic praise full of contrasts between the mighty and the lowly.
